# Welcome to DAI

## What you will learn this semester

- Build **client–server applications** with the Socket API (TCP, UDP).
- Master **HTTP** and deploy a real web infrastructure (reverse proxy,
  domain, HTTPS).
- Understand **email protocols** and implement a mail client.
- Use the tools of the trade: Git, GitHub, Docker, Maven, the terminal.

## How the course works

- Each week: short **cours** + long **labo** — you learn by doing.
- **Chapters** on the course site: theory, exercises + solutions,
  *Go further*.
- **3 practical works** in groups — subject of your choice.
- One communication channel: **GitHub Discussions**. No Cyberlearn, no
  Teams.
- Material in English; class and evaluations in French.

## Grading

- **Cours (80%)**: TE1 week 7 (**40%**) · TE2 week 16 (**60%**).
- **Labo (20%)**: the three practical works (report + deliverables,
  published rubrics).
- No exam session — everything happens during the semester.

## This week

- Environment verified (chapter 00 — every check passes).
- Join the course GitHub organization.
- Chapter 02: Git & GitHub, SSH keys, signed commits, Markdown.

# Git

## Why version control?

- Track every change, by everyone, forever — and undo mistakes.
- Work in parallel without overwriting each other.
- The single source of truth for your team's code.
- Git (2005, Linus Torvalds) is *the* VCS — everywhere in industry.

## Repositories and clones

- A **repository** = your project + its entire history.
- Git is **distributed**: every clone is a full copy — work offline.
- The copy on GitHub = the **remote** (`origin`).

## Commits

- A **commit** = a snapshot of the project, identified by its **hash**.
- History cannot be silently rewritten — hashes would change.
- **Tags** name important commits (releases).
- **Signed commits** prove authorship → "Verified" badge.

## The three areas

1. **Working directory** — the files you edit.
2. **Staging area** — what goes into the next commit (`git add`).
3. **Repository** — the committed history (`git commit`).

`git status` tells you where everything is.

## Branches and merging

- A **branch** = a movable pointer to a commit; `main` is the default.
- Feature work: branch off → commit → merge back.
- Three ways back: **merge** (default), **rebase** (linear history),
  **squash** (one commit).

## Conflicts

- Two people, same lines, same file → Git stops and asks **you**.
- Resolve: edit the markers, `git add`, conclude the merge.
- Not an accident — a normal part of teamwork. You will practice it
  today.

# GitHub

## More than hosting

- Hosts your repositories + adds collaboration: **issues**, **pull
  requests**, reviews, discussions.
- A social platform — your profile is a **portfolio**.
- Free Pro account with your HEIG-VD email (GitHub Education).

## The contribution cycle

1. Open an **issue** (describe the change).
2. Create a **branch**.
3. Commit, push.
4. Open a **pull request** — a teammate reviews.
5. Merge, delete the branch.

The workflow of your practical works — and of the industry.

## The rejected push

```text
! [rejected]  main -> main (fetch first)
```

- Not broken: a teammate pushed before you.
- Fix: `git pull`, resolve if needed, `git push`.
- Practice it **before** it happens under deadline pressure.

# Markdown

## Plain text that renders

- READMEs, protocol specs, PW reports — all written in **Markdown**.
- **Diffable**: Git shows which *sentence* changed. A `.docx` cannot.
- **Portable**: one file → readable text, GitHub page, PDF, slides.
- This deck and the whole course site are Markdown.

## The whole syntax

```markdown
# Heading      **bold**  _italic_  `code`

- bullet          1. numbered      > quote

[link](https://heig-vd.ch)   ![alt](diagram.png)

| Column | Column |
| ------ | -----: |
```

- Blank line separates blocks; a line break inside a paragraph is
  ignored.
- Fenced code blocks: three backticks **+ the language**.

## Which Markdown?

- **CommonMark** — the strict specification most tools follow.
- **GitHub Flavored Markdown** — CommonMark + tables, task lists,
  strikethrough. What you write for READMEs and issues.
